Add The New York Post on Google When al-Qaeda terrorists struck the World Trade Center on 9/11, six strangers found themselves trapped in an elevator in a desperate fight for survival. As the express elevator climbed to its first stop on the 67th floor, American Airlines Flight 11 plowed into the North Tower at 8:46 am, causing the elevator to shudder and free-fall down the shaft. One of the passengers pushed an emergency button, but the elevator had already plummeted 15 stories before stopping near the 50th floor. 4 A National Geographic docuseries premiering Aug. 21 reunites survivors of the 9/11 terrorist attacks on the Twin Towers 25 years later with the strangers and rescuers who changed their lives. National Geographic/Virginia Sherwood As a choking cloud of thick white smoke that smelled like chemicals began pouring into the cabin, panic wasn’t an option — it was a death sentence. So the six men — including a window cleaner and two Port Authority officials — calmly pooled their brains and their brawn. First, they worked together to open the stuck automatic metal doors with their hands. Explore More Mom shot 11-month-old son in the face so dad could never have custody: ‘Worth it’ Shrink who got into testy exchange with Lindsay Clancy’s lawyer while on the stand is ‘no longer employed’ Trump announces ‘biggest oil deal in world history’ with Venezuela to secure 65 billion reserve barrels But there was no exit on the other end — just a solid wall with the number “50” stenciled on it. Then, a burst of MacGyver-level ingenuity from someone always on the outside looking in at the WTC. Window cleaner and Polish immigrant Jan Demczur quickly whipped out the brass squeegee from the bucket by his feet and began frantically pecking at layers of drywall in a circular motion. Some of the others worked in tandem, punching and kicking the drywall until there was a hole large enough for everyone to crawl out. They landed in a men’s bathroom, where they met firefighters imploring them to leave. 4 John Paczkowski, George Phoenix and Jan Demczur (left to right) are reunited October 9, 2025 in Manhattan. The three previously worked in the North Tower of the World Trade Center and were stuck in an elevator together on 9/11. National Geographic/Virginia Sherwood So they rushed down 50 flights of stairs and bolted out of the North Tower at 10:23 AM. Five minutes later, the tower collapsed. Demczur reunited with two of the men — John Paczkowski and George Phoenix — as part of National Geographic’s new docuseries, “9/11 Reunited,” which premieres Aug. 21 at 8 p.m. The three-part series can also be streamed in its entirety the following day on Disney+ and Hulu. Both Paczkowski and Phoenix are filmed warmly embracing Demczur in a meet-up at a Manhattan bar, thanking him for helping save their lives. 4 Firefighters navigate the rubble of the World Trade Center on Sept. 11, 2001. Alamy Stock Photo “Seeing Jan and George again after all of these years reminded me of not only the tragedy of that day and the enduring grief we feel for all who were lost, but also the raw humanity of what we shared, how blessed we are to still be alive, and the responsibility we have to live life to its fullest,” Paczkowski told The Post The trio are among 14 survivors of the worst terror attack on US soil in history — which left 2,977 dead — who reunited with rescuers and other strangers who changed their lives for the docuseries. In the opening episode shared with The Post, both Paczkowski and Phoenix discussed how the Twin Towers held a special place in their hearts long before 9/11. 4 Deborah St. John, who was injured on 9/11 by a falling piece of an airplane. National Geographic/Virginia Sherwood Paczkowski, who worked on the 67 th floor as the Port Authority’s assistant director of operations, said working there was a “dream come true.” Phoenix, a PA senior engineer, recounted falling in love with his future wife, Martha, during a date at the WTC’s observation deck. The first episode also features Deborah St. John – who suffered severe injuries after being struck by debris from the second plane to hit the WTC on 9/11 – re-uniting with Stefan Horlacher, a stranger who rushed to her aid, administering first aid on the street amid mass chaos and flagging down an ambulance. “We knew that there were a significant number of 9/11 survivors who made deeply meaningful connections amidst the horror of 9/11 but, for a whole host of reasons, hadn’t seen each other since,” said director Julian Jones, who created the series in collaboration with the National September 11 Memorial & Museum and production company 72 Films. “In reaching out to the survivors, we became aware that many felt they had things they wanted to say but felt they couldn’t — until now. https://www.mediafax.ro/english/bogdan-i.text: Bogdan Ivan returns to the energy scandal after Bolojan accused him of alarmism In a Facebook post published Friday, Ivan claims that several large industrial consumers received notifications today warning them that they might be forced to limit their energy consumption. “As I pointed out yesterday, several major industrial consumers received notifications again today warning them that they might be forced to limit their energy consumption,” Bogdan Ivan stated. According to the former minister, the notifications reportedly caused concern among employees and management at some factories, as they were sent without a prior public explanation. Ivan states that he was contacted by representatives of several companies who wanted to know what would happen next and whether there was a risk that their operations would be affected. “People need clear answers, not dry documents that raise more questions than they answer,” Ivan wrote. The former minister once again criticizes Acting Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan and argues that the lack of public communication is fueling fears within the industry. „You see, Mr. Bolojan” “You see, Mr. Bolojan, this is what happens when things are kept out of the public eye and communicated only at the last minute,” Bogdan Ivan stated. The message comes after a heated exchange between Bogdan Ivan and Ilie Bolojan regarding the energy situation. Two days ago, Bolojan criticized the former minister after he publicly warned of a possible energy crisis and the situation facing large consumers. The interim prime minister argued that a potential restriction on consumption does not mean Romania is heading toward a blackout and described Ivan’s message as “irresponsible.” According to explanations provided by the authorities, the notifications sent to large consumers are part of existing procedures for situations in which the energy system reaches a critical point. A potential reduction in consumption does not automatically mean that companies will be disconnected. For now, however, Bogdan Ivan maintains that the notifications continue to be sent and that company representatives are concerned that industrial activity could be affected. https://www.dw.com/en/climate-change-and.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OF6J Aid organizations warn of an imminent collapse of Sudan's health system amid funding shortages Image: AFP Advertisement In Sudan , clashes between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have intensified in North Kordofan and parts of Blue Nile state. The fighting has forced thousands of civilians to flee amid the planting season. Since war broke out between the two factions and their allied militias in April 2023, both sides have fought for power . However, neither has managed to establish control over the entire country. The SAF, the nation's official army, is in control of Sudan's north and center, including the capital, Khartoum, while the RSF maintains its presence in the western Darfur region and parts of the south. The brutal war has plunged Sudan into one of the world's worst humanitarian and displacement crises, according to the United Nations and international aid organizations. The estimated death toll ranges from 40,000 to 250,000 people as reliable figures remain difficult to obtain amid the ongoing fighting . More than 12.4 million Sudanese have also been displaced, both within Sudan and to neighboring countries. Fighting between the RSF and SAF is prompting thousands of civilians to flee from their homes amid the planting season Image: Faiz Abubakr/Middle East Images/IMAGO This week, the aid organization Action Against Hunger sounded the alarm. "24.6 million people are experiencing high levels of acute food insecurity," Jan Sebastian Friedrich-Rust, executive director of the German section of the NGO, told DW. Friedrich-Rust added that an estimated 825,000 children younger than 5 suffer from severe acute malnutrition in 2026, while a total of 4.2 million children and pregnant or breastfeeding women are thought to be acutely malnourished. In October, the Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET) — which monitors food insecurity and uses the internationally recognized Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) system — also warned that several areas including camps for internally displaced people in Greater Darfur and Greater Kordofan, are expected to face Catastrophe (IPC Phase 5), the most severe classification of acute food insecurity. "The situation in Sudan continues to deteriorate and humanitarian needs are growing, even as the resources to respond are shrinking," Fabrizia Falcione, the Sudan representative of the United Nations Population Fund, the UN agency for sexual and reproductive health, said. "I recently visited the displacement camp Tawila and I am still struggling to find the words to describe what I witnessed," Falcione told DW. "Imagine a population larger than that of Frankfurt, Germany, forced to flee their homes and seek refuge in one place in less than three years." She added that more than 700,000 people there rely on just one hospital capable of performing Caesarean sections. Despite repeated warnings about the deteriorating humanitarian situation, the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan, which calls for $2.9 billion (€2.59 bn), is just 41% funded, with $1.2 billion (€1.07 bn) received from international donors so far. Community kitchen fights hunger in Sudan's Tawila camp To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Climate shocks exacerbate Sudan's humanitarian crisis The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) recently warned that extreme heat and heavy flooding are worsening the crisis in Sudan. "This year, a massive heatwave brought power cuts of up to 12 hours per day in some regions," Hager Ali, a Sudan researcher at the German Institute for Global and Area Studies (GIGA), told DW. "Riverbeds and dried-out fields are barren, which comes on top of the damage from combat, the RSF's scorched-earth tactics and environmental destruction." While the drought is affecting roughly half the country, heavy rains and localized flooding have worsened conditions in other areas of Sudan. "As if that wasn't enough, there is also a massive shortage of fertilizer and diesel," Ali told DW. Sudan relies on imported fertilizer and diesel shipped from the Persian Gulf through the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. However, amid the wider Iran war, Iran has been blocking shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, while the Iran-aligned Houthi rebels in Yemen have threatened and at times disrupted shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. "Fertilizer supply collapsed from 450,000 metric tons to only about 50,000" in 2026, Ali said, adding that a similar diesel shortage and the soaring cost of diesel compound the situation in two ways. "Agricultural equipment uses diesel and the transportation of humanitarian and agricultural goods within the country is getting a lot more expensive ," Ali said. In October, the International Food Policy Research Institute warned that staple food- and fuel prices in Sudan rose sharply in September 2026. Al-Harith Idriss Al-Harith Mohamed, Sudan's permanent representative to the United Nations, opposed an extension of the arms embargo across Sudan, citing disadvantages for the Sudanese Armed Forces Image: Luiz Rampelotto/EuropaNewswire/Sipa USA/picture alliance Limited arms embargo curbs hope for an end to the war Observers have long pointed out that the war in Sudan will not end until foreign backers stop supplying arms . The SAF is officially supported by Egypt, Turkey, Russia and Iran while the United Arab Emirates is alleged to be the RSF's main backer , a claim Abu Dhabi denies. However, in October, the UN Security Council extended the existing arms embargo only on Sudan's Darfur region until December 11, dropping calls for a nationwide embargo. "To expand the UN embargo across Sudan would have included drones in particular," Hager Ali said, noting that Sudan is one of the biggest theaters for drone warfare: As of 2026, the leading cause of civilian casualties in Sudan are drone strikes . She also told DW that Al-Harith Idriss al-Harith Mohamed, Sudan's permanent representative to the United Nations, opposed the extention of the embargo over concerns that it would disproportionately limit the Sudanese Armed Forces on the battlefield. "An arms embargo would deter potential backers from cooperating with the Sudanese Armed Forces, whereas the Rapid Support Forces don't necessarily source their weapons through official ways," Hager Ali said. "The RSF rely on trafficking with other militias, private military contractors and traders in the region," she said, adding that because the RSF obtains supplies from numerous sources and actors, it is difficult to target the group through a single embargo.
